terms.definition: The complete account of which values a variable takes across a set of observations and how often each value, or each interval of values, occurs.

A display of the distribution of one quantitative variable, built by dividing its range into adjacent equal-width intervals and drawing a bar over each interval whose height is the number of observations falling in it. Its bars touch because the intervals are adjacent slices of one continuous scale.

One of the equal-width intervals a histogram divides a quantitative range into. Bin width is chosen by whoever draws the chart and determines how much of the distribution's shape the picture can show.
The number of observations falling in a given category or bin.

A table listing each category or bin beside the number of observations in it, and often beside that count as a proportion of the total. It reports exact values that a chart of the same data can only be read to the nearest gridline.
A part divided by the whole it belongs to, so a value between 0 and 1. Thirteen of sixty people gives a proportion of 0.217, which the same fact reported as a percentage calls 21.7%.

alignment.note: PREM-QNT-003 defines a proportion as an equation asserting that two ratios are equal, such as a/b = c/d, which a learner solves for an unknown. This block uses the statistical sense: a part-to-whole fraction between 0 and 1 attached to a count. Both senses are standard and neither replaces the other; the surrounding context decides which is meant, and the concept scene bridges them where the word first appears here.

terms.definition: A display with one bar per category, the bar's length encoding a count or measured amount. Because a reader compares bars by comparing lengths, its numerical axis has to start at zero; gaps between the bars mark the categories as separate things.

A display that joins points measured in sequence, usually over time, so that the space between two points stands for the interval the quantity travelled through. It encodes a value by position rather than by length, so its vertical axis may be restricted to a stated range.

A display with one quantitative variable on each axis and one point per observation, used to ask whether the two measurements are related, whether any relationship is straight or curved, whether the spread of one changes across the other, and whether any point is unusual.

An observation lying far enough from the rest of the data to stand apart from them in a display. A histogram or scatter plot can flag one; whether it reflects the measurement, the record, or the person is a separate question the display cannot answer.

A numerical axis that begins somewhere other than zero, so that a bar shows only the part of its quantity above the starting value. On a bar chart this breaks the proportionality a reader relies on; on a display that encodes value by position, such as a line chart or scatter plot, a restricted range is defensible if it is clearly stated.
A pattern in which measured values or categories of two variables differ together in a sampled dataset; the pattern alone does not specify why it occurs.

alignment.note: PREM-SCI-007 owns this term and this lesson keeps its meaning unchanged. The only thing added here is the display that makes an association visible for two quantitative variables. Causal interpretation of an association remains the earlier lesson's territory, and the scatter scene points the learner back to it.
